V02-H-001: Shopkeepers often resist plans to close a street to cars, fearing that customers who cannot park outside will go elsewhere. In many towns where such schemes have gone ahead, the fear has proved exaggerated: people on foot linger, return more often and spend more over a month than drivers who stop briefly, and footfall on the closed street tends to rise. Yet the gains are not automatic. A pedestrian street works when it already sits within walking distance of homes, offices or public transport, so that people arrive on foot anyway. Where a high street serves mainly shoppers who drive in from scattered suburbs, closing it to traffic without offering another way to reach it can empty it, and the shopkeepers' fear turns out to be justified.
V02-H-002: Two drivers take the same corner too fast after the same glass of wine; one reaches home, the other strikes a cyclist who appears suddenly from a side lane. Most people blame the second driver far more, even though the two drivers made identical choices and differ only in what happened next, which neither controlled. This reaction sits uneasily with the widely held principle that people should be judged only for what is within their control. If we applied that principle strictly, we would have to say the drivers are equally culpable, and that our sharper condemnation of the second is a kind of error. The difficulty is that almost everything we do has consequences shaped by circumstance, so a strict rule of control would leave very little that anyone could be blamed or praised for at all.
V02-H-003: After learning the outcome of an event, people find it remarkably hard to recover how uncertain it looked beforehand. The outcome reorganises our memory of the evidence: signs that pointed towards it now seem obvious, while signs that pointed elsewhere fade or are reinterpreted as noise. As a result we tend to believe that we, and others, should have seen it coming. This matters most when we judge decisions. A doctor whose patient suffered a rare complication, or a manager whose project failed, is likely to be faulted for missing warnings that were, at the time, mixed in with many others pointing the opposite way.
V02-H-004: Lavish weddings are often criticised as a simple failure of prudence: families spend their savings, or borrow, for a single day that leaves nothing behind. The criticism misreads what the money buys. In many communities a wedding is the occasion on which a family displays its standing to a wide network of relatives, neighbours and future in-laws, and that standing affects the marriages its other children can make, the help it can call on and the credit it is offered. Seen this way, the spending is less a lapse than an investment in reputation. None of this makes it harmless. When every family must match its neighbours, the display that once signalled standing becomes a cost that all must pay merely to avoid falling behind, and the people least able to afford it are pressed hardest.
V02-H-005: It has become routine to dismiss the history of great individuals as naive, on the ground that leaders merely ride forces (economic, demographic, technological) that would have produced much the same results without them. The correction was needed, but it has been pushed too far. Structural forces set the range of what is possible; they rarely settle which possibility is realised. At moments of crisis, when institutions are weak and outcomes hang on a few decisions, the character and judgement of particular people can tip events one way or another, and the effects can last for generations. The sensible position is not to return to heroic biography but to ask, case by case, how wide the range left open by circumstance actually was, since that width determines how much any individual could matter.
V02-H-006: A standard textbook argument holds that raising the minimum wage must reduce employment, since employers buy less of anything that becomes more expensive. Comparisons of neighbouring areas where the wage floor rose in one and not the other have often found smaller job losses than that argument predicts, and sometimes none at all. One explanation is that where few employers compete for workers, wages were held below what a competitive market would pay, so a modest floor can raise pay without cutting jobs. But this evidence concerns modest increases in places where the floor was low relative to local wages. It says little about large rises, or about poorer regions where a single national floor sits close to the typical wage, and treating it as proof that minimum wages never cost jobs stretches it beyond what it shows.
V02-H-007: Port cities have long been more open to strangers than inland towns of similar size, and the usual explanation credits the sea with broadening minds. The cause is more practical. A port lives by trade with people it cannot choose, and its merchants, dock workers and officials learn that a ship's crew from a distant coast must be housed, fed, paid and understood if business is to continue. Tolerance there begins as a working habit, enforced by self-interest, before it becomes a value anyone defends. This also explains why such openness can be fragile. When trade declines or shifts to other harbours, the practical reason for accommodating outsiders weakens, and port cities have sometimes turned as suspicious of strangers as any inland town.
V02-H-008: It is sometimes said that a politician who lies to the public or bargains with a ruthless faction to prevent a greater harm has simply done the right thing, and that once the calculation favours the act, no moral residue remains. This tidy view misdescribes the situation. The act may be justified, all things considered, and still involve doing something wrong: deceiving people who were owed the truth, or lending strength to people who deserved none. A leader who felt nothing after such a choice would be more worrying than one who felt the weight of it, because that weight is how a person registers that a real claim was overridden rather than dissolved. Justification answers whether one should act; it does not erase what the act cost those it wronged.
V02-H-009: Early laboratory work on helplessness suggested a simple lesson: animals exposed to shocks they could not escape learned that nothing they did mattered, and later failed to escape even when escape became easy. The idea spread quickly into accounts of human depression and of children who stop trying at school. Later research reversed the emphasis. Passivity in the face of prolonged stress, it now appears, is the default response, and what is learned is the opposite: that one's actions can make a difference. Experiences of control teach organisms to override the default. The practical implication shifts accordingly. Rather than looking only for the damage done by uncontrollable events, one should ask whether a person has had enough experiences of mastery to learn that effort pays.
V02-H-010: Diners often praise a restaurant for serving the authentic version of a dish, meaning the one that matches how it is made in its place of origin. The standard is harder to apply than it sounds. Most celebrated dishes have changed repeatedly, absorbing ingredients that arrived through trade or conquest, and cooks in the same region disagree about the correct recipe. What is called authentic is usually one moment in that history, often the version a visitor first encountered, fixed and treated as the original. This does not make every claim of authenticity empty. A cook who learned a tradition from the inside and respects its logic is doing something different from one who merely borrows a name; but the difference lies in that understanding, not in matching a single correct recipe.
V02-H-011: A familiar account of why great empires fall points to overextension: they conquer more territory than they can defend or administer, and the cost of holding distant frontiers drains the centre. The account is attractive because it turns decline into a lesson about limits. Its weakness is that it is applied after the fact. Empires that collapsed are described as having overreached, while others that held equally vast and costly territories for centuries are not, and the difference is rarely explained by size alone. What seems to matter more is whether the centre could keep the loyalty of provincial elites and raise revenue without provoking revolt, capacities that some large empires possessed and some small ones lacked.
V02-H-012: Almost every company now publishes a mission statement, and most of them sound alike: commitments to customers, integrity, innovation and people. Because the words cost nothing and exclude nothing, they tell an outsider very little about how the firm will behave. A statement becomes informative only when it rules something out, when it commits the company to a choice that a competitor might reasonably make differently, such as refusing a profitable line of business or accepting slower growth for some stated reason. Statements of that kind are rare precisely because they constrain the people who write them, and that constraint is what gives them meaning.
V02-H-013: Capitals built from scratch, on open land chosen by the state, are usually judged against old capitals that grew over centuries, and they usually lose: their avenues are wide and empty, their ministries far apart, their street life thin. The comparison is partly unfair. An old capital is the survivor of many cities that never grew; the planned capital is judged in its first decades, before people have had time to adapt it to their purposes. Yet the unfairness cuts only so far. The features that make a planned capital feel lifeless (the separation of government from commerce, a scale designed for ceremony rather than walking) are fixed in its layout, and time can fill the spaces between buildings without changing how far apart they are.
V02-H-014: We defer to experts on bridges and medicines without hesitation, yet many people feel that deferring to someone else on a moral question (adopting a view on the ethics of eating meat simply because a thoughtful philosopher holds it) would be a failing. One explanation is that there are no moral experts to defer to. That seems too quick: some people have plainly thought harder and more carefully about such questions than others. A better explanation is that moral belief is meant to be connected to one's own understanding of why something is wrong; a person who refrains from cruelty only on someone's say-so seems to have the right belief in the wrong way. On this account deference may sometimes be prudent, when one must act and cannot work the question through, but it cannot be the end of the matter.
V02-H-015: Close-knit teams are often blamed for poor decisions, on the theory that members who like one another suppress doubts to preserve harmony. Yet many of the most effective teams are also highly cohesive, and their members argue fiercely because they trust that disagreement will not cost them their place. Cohesion, it seems, is not the culprit by itself. The trouble comes when cohesion is combined with a dominant leader who signals the preferred answer early, or with isolation from outside views, so that loyalty to the group comes to mean agreeing with it. Breaking up close teams to prevent bad decisions would therefore sacrifice the trust that makes candid disagreement possible.
V02-H-016: Fashion moves in cycles because it serves two opposed wishes at once: to resemble the people one admires and to stand apart from the people one does not. A style adopted by a small, admired group spreads as others imitate it; but the more widely it spreads, the less it distinguishes anyone, and the group that began it abandons it for something new. The style then lingers among late adopters until it seems dated, and it becomes available for revival only once it has been forgotten long enough to look fresh. The engine of change is therefore social rather than aesthetic: styles are dropped not because they stop being attractive but because they stop being distinctive.
V02-H-017: It seems natural to expect revolutions where misery is deepest, yet they have often broken out in societies that were growing richer and whose rulers had begun to reform. The puzzle dissolves once one considers what people compare their situation with. Long and settled hardship tends to produce resignation, because it is all that people expect. When conditions start to improve, expectations rise faster than conditions can, and when a reforming regime then stalls or reverses course, the gap between what people now think possible and what they actually have becomes intolerable. Discontent, on this view, tracks the distance between hopes and reality, not the absolute level of hardship.
V02-H-018: Money sent home by migrants now reaches many poor countries in larger sums than foreign aid, and it has advantages aid lacks: it goes directly to households, it tends to rise when the home country suffers a disaster, and it pays for food, school fees and medical care that families choose for themselves. It is tempting to conclude that remittances can do the work of development. The conclusion overreaches. Remittances smooth and raise household consumption, but they do not build roads, courts or power grids, and a country that comes to depend on exporting its workers may find that its most enterprising people, and the political pressure they might have exerted for reform, are abroad.
V02-H-019: When a poor neighbourhood starts to attract wealthier residents, the common fear is that existing tenants are driven out. Some careful tracking of households has found something less dramatic: long-standing residents of gentrifying areas move away at rates not much higher than those in similar neighbourhoods that are not changing, and those who stay benefit from safer streets and better shops. This finding is real but easy to misread. It concerns whether people leave, not who arrives. As rents rise, the poorer households who would have moved in, replacing those who leave for ordinary reasons, can no longer afford to, so the neighbourhood is transformed over a decade without any dramatic eviction. Displacement, in other words, may happen less at the door than in the queue for vacant homes.
V02-H-020: It is sometimes argued that we owe nothing to people who do not yet exist, since they cannot make claims on us and we cannot know what they will want. The second point is weaker than it looks. We do not know the tastes of people a century from now, but we know with some confidence that they will need breathable air, fertile soil and a climate in which crops grow, just as we do. Obligations of that basic kind do not depend on knowing anyone's particular preferences. And the first point proves too much: a person who buries a hazard that will harm whoever digs there in fifty years seems clearly to wrong that future person, even though no one yet exists to complain.
V02-H-021: People trying to build a habit usually rely on willpower and reminders, but habits form most reliably when a behaviour is repeated in the same setting, at the same time or after the same prompt, until the setting itself begins to trigger it. Once that link is established, the behaviour needs little deliberate effort; the cue does the work. This is why habits are often easiest to change when circumstances change anyway. Someone who moves house or starts a new job has lost many of the old cues at once, and for a while their routines are open to revision in a way they rarely are otherwise.
V02-H-022: Retirement is usually planned as a financial problem: whether savings will last. For many people the harder adjustment turns out to be of another kind. Work supplies more than income; it gives the week a shape, provides daily contact with people one did not choose but comes to rely on, and answers the question of what one does. Those who retire from jobs that supplied these things, and who have not built other sources of them, can find that a secure income leaves them oddly adrift. People whose sense of themselves was already rooted in family, hobbies or community tend to make the transition more easily, whatever their savings.
V02-H-023: Two responses are common when a celebrated figure from the past is found to have held views now regarded as abhorrent. One insists that such people be judged by the standards of their own time, since no one can be expected to see beyond the moral horizon of their age. The other holds that wrong is wrong, and that admiration should be withdrawn. Both overlook something. Any age contains dissenters, people who did see past the prevailing view, often at some cost, and their existence shows that the horizon was not closed. It does not follow that every figure who failed to join them was a villain; it does follow that 'they were of their time' is a partial excuse, which lessens blame without removing it.
V02-H-024: When cannon became powerful enough to batter down tall stone walls, the castle of a local lord lost much of its value as a refuge. The answer was a new kind of fortification: low, thick ramparts with angled bastions that deflected shot and allowed defenders to cover every approach. Such works were enormously expensive to build and to garrison, far beyond the means of most nobles, and so the ability to hold territory passed increasingly to rulers who could raise taxes across a whole realm. A change in military technology thus did political work, strengthening central authority at the expense of local power, not by any decision to centralise but through the rising cost of defence.
V02-H-025: Platforms that grow more valuable as more people use them, such as messaging services or marketplaces, are often said to be unassailable once they lead: every new user makes the leader more attractive, so challengers cannot catch up. The record is less kind to that claim. Leading platforms have lost their position when a rival offered something the leader could not easily match, or when users could belong to several platforms at once at little cost, so that joining a newcomer did not mean abandoning the old network. Network effects make leadership durable, not permanent; how durable depends largely on how costly it is for users to use more than one platform.
